section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department despatches, memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings from late 1933 to 1936 documenting communist and radical developments in Japan and adjacent regions. American diplomats, including Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and State Department specialist Eugene H. Dooman, report that orthodox communism in Japan is waning due to extensive police suppression, counter-propaganda by Christian and conservative groups, and public recantations by imprisoned leaders. At the same time, social and economic unrest among farmers and laborers is increasingly co-opted by reactionary military and fascist factions advocating national socialism under imperial sovereignty. Accompanying records track related communist investigations, educational purges, and anti-Soviet propaganda in Korea, Manchukuo, the Soviet Union, and Turkey.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of a diplomatic despatch evaluating recent communist developments, intellectual and judicial arrests, and public criticism of futile police suppression in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Concluding despatch segment: Communist regeneration crippled after the Omori bank robbery; arrests of Kawakami, Otsuka and judicial officials; an Asahi editorial urges free speech; radicalism reflects social unrest.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch on Communist Developments and Judicial Arrests

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a memorandum on the growth of communism in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: File note on Salisbury's June 25, 1933 memorandum: communism's increase in Manchukuo is thought to prepare an eventual government under Japanese communism.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum on Manchukuo Communism (894.00B/53)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 596 and contrasting the prospects of communism versus national socialism in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reviews Despatch No. 596: communism has declined among students, rightist groups have stolen its thunder, and Japan, if capitalism fails, will turn to national socialism rather than communism.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 596 Regarding Communism in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic report detailing the decline of communism in Japan, Christian counter-campaigns, police roundups, and the ascendance of reactionary nationalism.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Despatch No. 596 provides an exhaustive assessment of communism in Japan, concluding that the movement is on the decline despite sensational press coverage of police roundups. It analyzes student radicalism and explains how educational campaigns organized by Christian bodies such as the YMCA successfully diminished communist influence in universities. The report explains that rural peasants and factory workers are increasingly drawn to patriotic reactionary and fascist groups that borrow socialist economic tenets while venerating the Emperor. It also reviews the arrests of Zenkyo unionists, the heavy representation of Koreans in radical labor activities, and the controversial prison recantations ('reforms') of communist leaders.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 596: 'Communism in Japan'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 607 regarding police arrests of 1,696 suspected radicals.
subfiles.summary: File note on Despatch No. 607 (December 11, 1933): 1,696 persons arrested as radicals between February and November 1933.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 607 on Radical Arrests (894.00B/55)

subfiles.about: Extract from Periodic Report No. 72 covering the lifting of a press ban on Zenkyo arrests and cumulative communist arrest statistics from 1928 to 1933.
subfiles.summary: Extract from Despatch No. 607: after a press ban lifted November 20, 1933, 1,696 Zenkyo members were shown arrested; over 29,000 sympathizers handled 1928-1933, including three judges and five clerks.
subfiles.title: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 607 (Periodic Report No. 72): Section on Communism

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum discussing an interview with former communist leader Katsumaro Akamatsu on the rise of nationalism in Japanese labor.
subfiles.summary: Dooman on Despatch No. 628: Japan's communal orientation favors national socialism, shown by former communist leader Akamatsu's embrace of the Oriental view of the empire as one family.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 628 Regarding Views of Former Communist Leader

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a Japan Advertiser press interview with former communist labor leader Katsumaro Akamatsu.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits a December 19, 1933 Japan Advertiser interview with Katsumaro Akamatsu, once a communist leader, whose nationalism reflects working-class radical thought.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 628: Transmitting Newspaper Interview of Former Communist Leader

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping interview with Katsumaro Akamatsu explaining why international Marxism has failed in Japan and why trade unions have turned nationalistic.
subfiles.summary: Interview with Akamatsu: over 95 percent of Japanese unions embraced nationalism, internationalism failed, and he contrasts Western liberal individualism with the Oriental view of the state as an imperial family.
subfiles.title: Clipping from The Japan Advertiser: 'Japanese Laborers Turn Nationalistic'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 656 regarding communist arrests and indictments in Korea.
subfiles.summary: File note on Despatch No. 656 (January 9, 1934): twenty-nine communists arrested in Korea, twenty-two indicted.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 656 on Communist Arrests in Korea (894.00B/57)

subfiles.about: Extract from Periodic Report No. 73 detailing the arrest of radical schoolteachers in Korea and primary school educators in Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Extract: Korea press ban lifted revealing twenty-nine radical arrests, twenty-two indicted for teaching communism through textbooks; Osaka police detained five teachers for a radical education institute.
subfiles.title: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 656 (Periodic Report No. 73): Note on Communism
